Threat.value: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.

issues.explanation: Occupation 'Retired' is implausible for age 28 (retired is implausible if age < 50).

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within Memory, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' sits awkwardly with 'my memories are very clear and detailed' and 'mostly pictures or images' for a PTSD profile tied to a life-threatening accident; this pattern suggests unusually easy verbal processing despite vivid intrusive-style memory, which weakens coherence of the memory node.

issues.item: Threat: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
issues.explanation: The threat item about repeatedly checking whether someone is following him implies an interpersonal pursuit/assault-type danger theme, which is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma being a life-threatening accident and with the rest of the profile, which does not otherwise indicate persecution-related threat.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me
issues.explanation: 'I dwell on what other people have done to me' also implies an interpersonal harm/blame theme that does not fit well with the accident trauma context or the other selected appraisals, memories, and threats.

issues.item: Undereating: I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping
issues.explanation: Restricting food as a coping strategy is not well supported by the rest of the profile. The other items describe accident-related sensory threat (loud sounds, startle), image-based trauma memory, and self-critical appraisals, with maladaptive responses centered on avoidance/removal from reminders and rumination/meaning seeking. Undereating introduces a qualitatively different coping pattern that is not reflected elsewhere in Triggers, Threat, Memory, or Negative Appraisals, making it the least clinically coherent item in this five-component profile.

vignette:
Martin, a 52-year-old film director in a long-term relationship, came to treatment after a slow, uneasy change in himself following a life-threatening accident on a night location shoot. The accident had happened when he was standing near a set rigging in a warehouse darkened for a scene; a heavy piece of equipment gave way without warning, and in the seconds before impact he had been thrown against metal and pinned in chaos, hearing shouted orders, the scrape of machinery, and the sharp, unexpected crashes that seemed to come from everywhere at once. What remained most strongly for him were not words but pictures: the angle of the beam, the glare of work lights, a flash of someone running toward him, the feeling that the scene had become unreal and terrifyingly clear all at once. He said he could not put the event into a proper story, only into fragments and images that arrived with startling detail. In the months that followed, he began to look at himself through the disaster, convinced that the person he had become was unrecognisable to him and that the way he had reacted in the aftermath proved he was a lousy coper, inadequate for the work and for the people who relied on him. Those judgments did not stay abstract; they shaped what he did. He started avoiding circumstances that reminded him of the accident, turning down evening calls that would require him to be in darkened sound stages and finding excuses not to visit sets once lighting tests had begun. He also threw himself into distraction, filling gaps in the day with editing, scrolling, and constant background noise, and he kept thinking about why the event had happened to him, as if some explanation might restore a sense of order. But the more he stayed away from dark, cramped, noisy places, the more he noticed the event as a sequence of vivid images when he least expected it, as though the mind had preserved it in pictures precisely because he had not been able to give it words. Those images fed the same harsh conclusions: if he could still be ambushed by fragments of that night, then he was fragile, not in control, and not the man he had believed himself to be.

Martin also came to live in a state of persistent watchfulness. The accident had taught him to expect danger in sudden sound, so loud noises and even ordinary abrupt sounds at home or on set could make him jump before he had time to think. He found himself on guard whenever a door slammed in the apartment, when a dropped prop rang out on location, or when a car backfired outside a restaurant, his body already bracing before his mind had caught up. Because he had come to believe he was inadequate and a bad coper, he monitored his surroundings for signs that something could fail, and that self-doubt made every unexpected noise feel like confirmation that he was not safe and not capable of handling another shock. At the same time, the memory itself seemed to keep the threat alive: the clearer the visual fragments became, the more his body reacted as if the warehouse were present again, and the more alert he became to sounds that resembled the crash and shouting of that night. He described getting through work by staying busy, checking equipment obsessively, and arranging his days to avoid being in the dark, but those efforts carried their own cost. The more he distracted himself and kept away from reminders, the less he trusted his own reactions, and the more unrecognisable he felt. He became more guarded with his partner, less willing to linger after work, and more likely to cut short social plans if there was any chance of being caught in a dim theatre, a loading bay, or a quiet street after dusk. Even in those safer moments, his attention kept snapping toward sound, scanning for what might go wrong next. By the time he sought help, he was worn down by the feeling that he was living in the aftermath of an event he could not fully describe, held together by avoidance and distraction, while his own mind kept supplying the same hard verdicts about his inadequacy. What brought him in was the fear that his life would keep shrinking around those pictures and startle responses, and his hope was that he might finally make sense of what happened without being trapped by it.
